questions.title: Does Louisiana law require a physical signature on the premium finance company’s “certification” of cancellation?
questions.question_body: In Williams v. GoAuto Insurance the Fifth Circuit says that the statute only requires a “statement certifying” certain facts and finds no authority that a signature is required. I’m confused because some Louisiana cases (e.g., Benitez v. Elsayed) criticize the lack of a signed employee name. How should a lower court determine whether a signature is mandatory under La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(a)? Does “certifying” imply a signed statement, or is an unsigned electronic notice sufficient?

questions.title: How is the term “receipt” in La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i) interpreted for modern electronic communications?
questions.question_body: The court relied on Black’s Law Dictionary to say receipt can be satisfied by electronic delivery to GoAuto’s computer system, but the statute was drafted before widespread use of web services. Is there any Louisiana precedent defining “receipt” for electronic mail or web‑service calls, and does the insurer need physical possession of a paper document for the cancellation to be valid?

questions.title: What is the legal significance of a “private carrier” under the cancellation statute, and can e‑mail be treated as a private carrier?
questions.question_body: The district court held that an APAC employee delivering the notice via e‑mail qualifies as a private carrier, citing Huntley v. Bayer MaterialScience. I’m unsure how the private‑carrier concept applies to electronic transmission. Does Louisiana case law support treating e‑mail or a web‑service call as a private carrier for purposes of the cancellation notice?

questions.title: When can a federal appellate court certify a question of Louisiana law to the state Supreme Court?
questions.question_body: The Fifth Circuit denied the plaintiffs’ request for certification, referencing Jefferson v. Lead Indus. Ass’n. What standards does a federal court apply when deciding whether to certify a question of state law, especially when the issue (e.g., “receipt”) has not been decided by the Louisiana Supreme Court?

questions.title: Does the timing of the APAC employee’s signature stamp affect the validity of the cancellation under Louisiana law?
questions.question_body: In the opinion, the signature stamp is affixed after the policy is automatically cancelled by GoAuto’s computer system. If the statute required the certification to occur before cancellation, would the timing of the stamp render the cancellation ineffective, or does the electronic certification suffice regardless of when a human signs?

questions.title: How does Louisiana’s “strict adherence” requirement interact with technological automation in insurance cancellations?
questions.question_body: The court emphasizes strict adherence but also accepts fully automated e‑mail and web‑service processes. Are there any Louisiana cases that address whether a fully automated cancellation process meets the “strict adherence” mandate, or is this a novel interpretation by the Fifth Circuit?

questions.title: What is the role of the “minimum time to cure” function in the cancellation statute, and did GoAuto satisfy it?
questions.question_body: The statute aims to provide a clear cancellation date and a minimum cure period. The opinion mentions a ten‑day notice to the insured. Did the court consider whether GoAuto’s automated system properly accounted for the statutory cure period, and how is that period measured when the notice is sent electronically?
